name: Cloud Engineer Roadmap
tagline: From Linux and DNS to reproducible, observable, cost-aware cloud infrastructure
summary: An ordered path for engineers who build and run infrastructure on a public cloud. It begins below the cloud — Linux, networking, certificates — because every managed service is an abstraction over those, then covers the four primitives every provider sells under different names: identity, network, compute and storage. The second half is what separates a working account from an operable platform: describing everything as code, automating delivery, handling secrets, measuring reliability against an SLO, and keeping the bill proportional to the traffic.

steps.label: Linux
steps.note: Almost every instance, container and managed runtime is Linux, so processes, permissions, systemd and the shell are the floor you debug down to.

steps.label: DNS
steps.note: Comes early because service discovery, certificate validation, failover and 'it works from my laptop' all resolve to DNS records and their TTLs.

steps.label: TLS & certificates
steps.note: Every public endpoint terminates TLS somewhere; knowing chains, SNI and renewal prevents the single most common self-inflicted outage.

steps.label: Git & version control
steps.note: Learned before any automation, because from here on the desired state of your infrastructure lives in a repository and changes go through review.

steps.label: Cloud provider fundamentals
steps.note: Regions, availability zones, the shared responsibility model, quotas and the console-versus-API split are the vocabulary every later step is expressed in.

steps.label: IAM & least privilege
steps.note: Placed before compute on purpose: identity is the real perimeter in the cloud, and roles granted early as wildcards are almost never narrowed later.

steps.label: Networking & VPC
steps.note: Subnets, route tables, NAT and security groups decide what can reach what; nearly all 'connection timed out' incidents are answered in this layer.

steps.label: Load balancing
steps.note: The first component in front of your application: it defines health checks, TLS termination and how a rolling deploy avoids dropping requests.

steps.label: Object storage
steps.note: The default place for anything that is not a database row — uploads, artefacts, backups, logs — and the cheapest durable storage the cloud sells.

steps.label: Docker
steps.note: Containers make the deployable unit identical from laptop to production, which is the prerequisite for every orchestrator and managed runtime that follows.

steps.label: Kubernetes
steps.note: Worth learning after containers and networking, since it mostly composes those primitives; learn it to understand scheduling, not because every workload needs it.

steps.label: Serverless
steps.note: The other end of the spectrum from a cluster you operate: study it next to Kubernetes so the choice becomes a trade-off about cold starts, limits and cost rather than a preference.

steps.label: Infrastructure as code
steps.note: Comes only once you know what the resources are, because clicking in a console teaches you the model but leaves nothing reviewable or reproducible.

steps.label: Terraform
steps.note: A concrete tool for the previous idea: providers, state, plan-before-apply and modules are the day-to-day mechanics of changing infrastructure safely.

steps.label: CI/CD
steps.note: With code and infrastructure both in Git, a pipeline becomes the only path to production — which is also where policy checks and plan approvals belong.

steps.label: Secrets management
steps.note: Automation immediately creates the problem of credentials in pipelines and repos; short-lived, rotatable secrets issued to workload identities are the answer.

steps.label: Observability
steps.note: Once deploys are frequent you need metrics, logs and traces to tell whether a change helped, and to answer questions you did not anticipate.

steps.label: SLOs & error budgets
steps.note: Turns raw telemetry into a decision rule: how much unreliability is acceptable, and therefore when to ship features versus stop and fix.

steps.label: Capacity planning
steps.note: With targets defined you can size things deliberately — headroom, autoscaling limits and quota ceilings — instead of reacting to the next traffic spike.

steps.label: Cost management
steps.note: Last because it depends on everything above: in the cloud an architecture choice is a recurring bill, and tagging, rightsizing and commitment discounts are engineering work.
